world_status: accessible description is silent on stress
sweep_summary: Baka (Cameroon) is not in the catalog. All three stress-title hits attached to baka1272 by Glottolog are computerized keyword misassignments (language code 'computerized assignment from \"harry\"' for the two book reviews by Hyman & Wilson 1991 and Wei 2019; 'from \"ideal\"' for Revithiadou 1999, a dissertation on Greek/Russian/Salish lexical accent). None concerns Baka; priority none for all. The only Baka-specific prosody statement read (Djoupee 2001 §7.f.2, PDF p. 50) says loanword stress from French/English is mapped onto Baka tones, i.e. it is silent on native word stress; Djoupee 2017 §2.3 describes a three-tone lexical system with no mention of stress. Still unread and the best candidates for an explicit statement: Phillips 1981 'A phonology of Baka' (SIL Yaoundé, could not be reached by automated download), Kilian-Hatz 1995 §2.1.3 'Töne und Intonation' (print only; TOC held by the project) / Kilian-Hatz 2000 English grammar (SIL). [...] The corpus shows the existence of three phonetic level tones: high (H) with 507 occurrences, low (B) with 829 occurrences and mid (M) with 40 occurrences. Ils doivent leur statut phonologique à 29 oppositions (avec 9 incluant le ton moyen).."; p…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Baka is a three-tone register language (H, L, marginal M; only open CV syllables; nouns carry lexical tone, verbs do not). The most authoritative modern description (Djoupee 2017) and the earlier MA thesis (Djoupee 2001, following Phillips 1981) treat tone as the only word-prosodic system and make no statement at all about word stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; tone: mid tone is rare (39-40 lexical items), verbs have no lexical tone, tone sandhi in nominal morphology (Djoupee 2001).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical (word-level) tone analysis on a 1423-item lexicon of citation forms; no phrase-level stress or intonation statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Djoupee 2017 describes the Baka of the Haut-Nyong department, East Region, Cameroon (baka1272 proper; ISO bkc), from a spontaneous-speech corpus; Djoupee 2001 is the same Cameroon variety. Paulin 2010 (not opened) covers the Gabon (Minvoul) Baka. Glottolog's Rénaud 1976 entry is a misassignment (Bajele/Gyele, a Bantu language of Bipindi, not Baka).

new_statements.quote: Au niveau suprasegmental. Sur le plan prosodique, l'accent tonique de la langue source correspond aux tons ci-après: -Ton haut (anglais) ma'chine [misini]; (français) pa'paye [papaye]; -Ton bas (français) café [kapi] café; (anglais) cup-board [kʌbɔ:] armoire
new_statements.translation: At the suprasegmental level. On the prosodic plane, the word stress of the source language corresponds to the following tones: High tone: (English) ma'chine [misini]; (French) pa'paye [papaye]; Low tone: (French) café [kapi]; (English) cup-board [kʌbɔ:] 'cupboard'
new_statements.citation: Djoupee, Bertille. 2001. Morphologie nominale du Baka. Mémoire de maîtrise, Université de Yaoundé I. 103 pp.
new_statements.locator: §7.f.2 'Au niveau suprasegmental', PDF p. 50 of 103 (loanword phonology; no printed page number on the scan)
new_statements.reading: Weak, indirect evidence only: in French/English loans the source-language stress is re-interpreted as lexical tone, consistent with Baka being a tone language without a word-stress system. Djoupee 2017 (thesis, §2.3 pp. 53-55, already held by the project) describes three lexical tones (H/B/M) and never mentions stress or accent; Kilian-Hatz 1995 has a section 'Töne und Intonation' (§2.1.3, TOC only held by the project). No first-hand source read in this search of works with stress in the title states a word-stress position for Baka, and none of the three works with stress in the title concerns Baka at all.
new_statements.found_by: works with stress in the title

new_statements.quote: Le baka comprend 3 tons. Le ton haut est marqué par l'accent aigu (á, í, ɔ́, etc.), le ton moyen n'a pas d'accent (a, i, ɔ, etc.), et le ton bas est marqué par l'accent grave (à, ì, ɔ̀, etc.). [...] Les tons s'écrivent généralement tels qu'ils sont prononcés. [...] La majorité des verbes s'écrivent avec un ton moyen suivi d'un ton bas, comme dans kindà envoyer et sià voir. [§6, p. 4:] Les tons sont importants seulement lorsqu'ils changent le sens d'un mot comme dans l'exemple ci-dessous : kòbo cadavre kóbo sauterelle kobo ancien
new_statements.translation: Baka has 3 tones. The high tone is marked by the acute accent (á, í, ɔ́, etc.), the mid tone has no accent mark (a, i, ɔ, etc.), and the low tone is marked by the grave accent (à, ì, ɔ̀, etc.). [...] Tones are generally written as they are pronounced. [...] Most verbs are written with a mid tone followed by a low tone, as in kindà 'send' and sià 'see'. [§6:] Tones matter only when they change the meaning of a word, as in the example below: kòbo 'corpse', kóbo 'grasshopper', kobo 'old/elder'.
new_statements.citation: Léonard, Yves. 2009. Orthographe Baka. Yaoundé: SIL Cameroon.
new_statements.locator: §3 'Les tons', printed pp. 1-2 (PDF pp. 3-4 of 10); §6 printed p. 4 (PDF p. 6)

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's existing statements (Djoupee 2017 §2.3: three lexical tones H/B/M, no mention of stress; Djoupee 2001 §7.f.2: loanword stress reinterpreted as tone). Same three-level tone system, same silence on stress. Identity: 'langue parlée par plus de 50 000 Bakas dans la Province de l'Est du Cameroun' (p. 1) = baka1272 [bkc], Cameroon variety.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A three-level lexical tone language (high, mid, low), with tone contrasts on both nouns and verbs, floating tones, and grammatical tone changes on verbs (tense, object). The ten-page orthography statement says nothing about word stress, accent d'intensité or prominence; the only occurrences of 'accent' are the names of the diacritics (accent aigu, accent grave). No word-stress position can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: most verbs are M-L (kindà, sià) with rare L-M exceptions (dòto 'stay', lɛ̀ji 'leave'); monosyllabic verbs are normally mid-toned (ja 'take') with rare exceptions (jɛ̀ 'hear'); some syllables have been lost but leave floating tones that are not written (p. 2). Every syllable ends in a vowel except in some loanwords (§2.2, p. 2).
new_statements.identity_note: Léonard 2009 explicitly concerns the Baka of the East Province of Cameroon (over 50,000 speakers), the same variety as Djoupee 2017/2001 and the catalog record (baka1272 [bkc]). Paulin 2010 (not readable) concerns the Gabon variety (Makokou and Minvoul regions, fewer than 1,000 speakers), which shares the ISO code but is treated by Paulin as a distinct variety (§2.2.3.1 'La variété gabonaise confrontée à celle du Cameroun'); any future reading of it should be flagged as Gabon Baka. Brisson 2010 is subtitled 'Sud-Cameroun' (Cameroon variety).
